name: Fon Vodun

dating.dating_summary: Aja-Fon migration from Tado is dated by comparative Gbe-language linguistics and oral-tradition triangulation to roughly the 12th-13th century CE; Vodun-type practice is inferred to predate the Dahomey kingdom itself (founded c. 1645) but no scholar-verified specific date was found beyond "predates the 17th-century kingdom" — the state-sponsored Mawu-Lisa cult specifically is a datable 1740s political act, not deep antiquity.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: No durable ritual architecture/inscriptions predate the 17th century; material culture is largely perishable — effectively absent as independent physical dating evidence.

earliest_written_attestation.note: European documentation from 17th-century contact; sustained Dutch/French/British/Danish documentation from the 17th-18th centuries. A specific 1658 Doctrina Christiana citation for early Vodun awareness could not be independently verified in this research pass — flagged, not asserted.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: Melville J. Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (J.J. Augustin, 1938), based on 1931 fieldwork — the foundational modern ethnography.

tradition_internal_claim.note: Migration narrative from Tado (Mono River) via Allada to Abomey, tied to the Agassou (leopard-ancestor) foundational myth.

estimated_oral_origin.method: Comparative Gbe-language historical linguistics plus oral-tradition triangulation.

notes: Nana Buluku (primordial figure who withdrew after birthing the twin deities Mawu/moon-night-female and Lisa/sun-day-male, who fuse into composite Mawu-Lisa) — a deus-otiosus pattern better fitting henotheism than monotheism, since worship in practice centers on the accessible vodun (Sakpata/earth, Sogbo-Xevioso/thunder, Agbe/sea, etc.). No named academic source was found directly adjudicating the monotheism-vs-henotheism classification dispute — flagged as this project's own tag judgment, not a cited scholarly consensus.
